ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: A holeless iron hammer is a solid, unusable hammer-head image; separately, the phrase can be applied as a label to a person.
EvidenceBody: An impossible solid hammer-head with no eye through which a handle could be fitted; the phrase calls this imagined object ‘iron,’ but does not document an actual manufactured tool. The phrase occurs 256 times in 108 allowlisted texts. Chan records repeatedly deploy this unusable hammer as an image of something offering no point of entry. Fachang Yiyu says that water cannot wet it and wind cannot enter it, ‘like a holeless iron hammer’ (水灑不著。風吹不入。如箇無孔鐵鎚相似). Huguo Cian Jingyuan gives it as the direct answer to ‘What thing can heaven not cover and earth not support?’ Xuedou Chongxian's verse speaks of ‘a holeless iron hammer driving in a wedge again’ (無孔鐵鎚重下楔), and Yuanweng Xin calls the whole ten-direction world such a hammer while denying any place for conjecture. These are deployments of the solid object-image, distinct from passages that directly call people holeless iron hammers.

DraftEvidence.ZenBend: A holeless iron hammer is a solid, unusable hammer-head image; separately, the phrase can be applied as a label to a person.
DraftEvidence.CounterexampleOrLimit: Primary Zen-loaded sense first. The ordinary bridge is mechanical: a hammer-head needs an eye for its handle, so this imagined solid head is unusable as a normal hammer. The corpus's own water, wind, wedge, and no-place predicates establish the no-entry deployment; the entry does not assign it an invisible symbolic meaning. No harvested passage treats the compound as an actual implement.

ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: This separate sense denotes a person called a ‘holeless iron hammer’, not a solid hammer-head with no handle-eye.
EvidenceBody: The same compound also directly labels people rather than merely comparing another object or statement with a hammer. Masters address an assembly as “this squad of holeless iron hammers” (這一隊無孔鐵鎚), dismiss a non-answering visitor with “Holeless iron hammer—go to the hall!”, and say that two old masters are “a pair of holeless iron hammers.” Here the grammatical referent is a person or pair of people, so this person-label is split from the object-image rather than blurred into one gloss.
